comment_text.value:
Hey @luis_valerio, kevan here! That question shaped most of the design.

We assume you can't reliably stop the model from being prompt injected. So nothing is enforced at the model layer. Enforcement happens at the proxy, which sits between the agent and the downstream API and is the only thing holding the credential. The agent never sees the key, so an injected agent can't bypass it or route around the deterministic policy.

For irreversible actions you stack three things:

1. Method/endpoint restrictions. "This agent may only GET under /instances/*" means a DELETE never reaches the provider. For infra agents we'd push read-only by default and allowlist the few mutations you need.

2. Human-in-the-loop on the dangerous ops. Approval can be required conditionally: on DELETE, on specific operations, or when a parameter matches (resource outside the allowed set, etc). The request is frozen server-side, so what the approver sees is exactly what executes. The agent can't swap the payload after the yes.

3. Audit logs on every call, including denials, with the agent and end-user identity attached. So you can see the agent tried a DELETE it wasn't allowed, on whose behalf, and with what body.

Basically we treat every call like a compromised laptop: don't assume it behaves, scope the credential, and gate the risky actions behind a second party. Would love to hear more about your setup.

story_title.value: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents

comment_text.value:
>Your job is to design, the AI builds like the junior engineers. Then you review their work.

I'll add to this that your job is also to design tooling and feedback loops that allows the AI to improve over time.

You have policy gates: How the AI should act. (and a feedback loop to check the code is adhering to those policy gates)

You have quality gates: How the AI verifies it's done things correctly (testing, linting, PRDs, cyclomatic complexity)

Modern AI engineering is really about improving this system rather than manually reviewing AI output. The better the policy gate and quality gate enforcement, the less manual review is required and the more velocity you achieve.

Sticking with being a human-in-the-loop reviewer of AI code is where people lose all hope in still being software engineers.

story_title.value: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?

This is how I view it. If you're going to be hosting dozens or hundreds of sites having a consistent platform like this is important even if Claude Code is doing all of the implementation work. It has understood and workable flows for things like content approval, timed releases, etc. All the things people think about when they talk about "managing content" and for the most part organizations still want human in the loop, especially for gated approvals and auditability.

If I'm thinking of building a single one off site, then yeah I'd probably opt to just let CC handle it without worrying about a framework which is overengineered for my current need. That's what I do with most of the personal projects I work on these days. But I do have a skill to build consistency around the parts that should be consistent for everything I host. Like package shape and types of hooks available for deployment. How sites are publicly exposed and DNS management.

comment_text.value:
Hey HN,

Over the past few months, we’ve watched autonomous agents transition from conversational LLMs into tool-wielding operators equipped with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, terminal execution, filesystem access, and web scrapers.

The vulnerability: once an agent has tool execution capabilities, any untrusted data it touches (web scrapes, emails, customer tickets) becomes an active attack vector. System prompts fail against 70%+ of indirect prompt injections, Unicode steganography, and SSRF payloads (targeting 169.254.169.254 AWS metadata or IPv4-mapped IPv6 loopbacks).

We built Tcha Protection (MIT, npm install -g tcha-protection) to solve this deterministically at the transport and STDIO proxy layer, rather than relying on probabilistic LLM system prompts.

### What it does: Tcha sits as a transparent, sub-millisecond reverse proxy between your host agent (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, custom agents) and MCP tool servers:

1. In-Line MCP Reverse Proxy: Intercepts tools/call JSON-RPC streams in flight with <= 1ms latency overhead. If a call targets path traversal (../../etc/shadow), unapproved destructive mutations, or forbidden egress, Tcha parries the request immediately with standardized JSON-RPC error -32001 before the downstream server is touched. 2. SSRF & Cloud Metadata Shield: Resolves DNS hostnames and strictly blocks requests targeting AWS/Azure/GCP metadata (169.254.169.254, fd00:ec2::254), IPv4-mapped IPv6 loopbacks (::ffff:127.0.0.1), hex/octal/decimal IP encodings, and RFC-1918 private subnets. 3. Unicode Steganography & Delimiter Sanitizer: Detects and neutralizes zero-width unicode injections (\u200B, \uFEFF), ASCII smuggling via Unicode tags, and multi-modal delimiter breakouts ([INST], <|im_start|>). 4. Cryptographic Merkle Audit Ledger: Every tool execution, parameter hash, and intercept decision is written to an append-only SQLite WAL ledger with continuous SHA-256 Merkle link chaining. 5. HMAC Human-in-the-Loop (HITL): High-risk mutating actions (e.g. rm -rf, DROP TABLE) trigger an HMAC challenge requiring human sign-off. 6. Compliance Crosswalk: Maps neutralized vectors directly to the EU AI Act (Article 15), SOC 2 Type II (CC6.1), and OWASP Top 10 for LLMs.

### Benchmark & Performance: - 100-Probe Red-Team Suite: Tested against 100 categorized adversarial attack vectors across prompt injection, steganography, SSRF, traversal, and tool abuse. 100/100 attacks neutralized (0 escapes). - Latency Overhead: Sub-millisecond (average < 1.0ms per tool invocation).

### Quickstart: Run the 100-probe adversarial audit locally: $ npx tcha-protection audit

Or wrap any MCP server: $ tcha wrap npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem ./data

- Live Site: https://tcha.dev - Verified Audit Report: https://tcha.dev/report.html - GitHub Repo (MIT): https://github.com/Tchapwo1/tcha

We would love HN's brutal feedback on our parser, our SSRF CIDR deny-lists, and what edge cases in MCP tool calling we should test next.

comment_text.value:
The reason we fell first is because we embraced the copilots. We used them heavily, this gave them more and more training data on top of the code they slurped up from our using their assistants. Soon the assistant became the agent who killed the human.

They also had a rich starting point from open source code (which we somehow gave up without realising it). All of this won't happen as efficiently for these other fields, but it will happen, much in the way you've described. We (swes) turned out to be a rather dumb group of people, which is hilarious since we think we're clever.

The only moat we have is the human to human element, we need to talk to other humans in the business. Customers, etc. But once they're replaced by machines or automation, then machine to machine communication will be the preferred mode of communication and work and the legacy humans will be increasingly cut out of the loop. Human in the loop is a death sentence we just don't realise it.

so first off, i'm not an AI avoider - i use LLMs all day at work, and have several personal projects i'm likewise using claude for. but a single, interactive session produces code as fast as i can handle, if i want to keep a tight rein on the quality of the output - i often find myself having to look at the code generated from some intermediate stage and course-correct.

i do use agents for code review but again in a very human-in-the-loop manner; i will ask for a review and then read it over before feeding it to my coding LLM session and asking it to read and iterate on it. as you say, it can be surprisingly tricky to get right, and i like the confidence of the human being the coordinating reviewer.

thanks for all the examples, though - that does give me a lot more context for what people mean by "software factories" (and the assurance that they don't fit the way i work).

comment_text.value:
A couple, yes, but I wouldn’t say it’s a ton of companies.

These stories were popular during the period when people didn’t understand how AI worked or what was possible. It was feasible to produce fake demos that relied on humans doing the work because few people understood how AI worked. If your demo took an input and produced an output 1 to 12 hours later with variable delay nobody questioned it because they didn’t know what AI looked like. They thought maybe that’s how long the computers had to think or that there was a single computer working through a backlog.

Now everyone has used ChatGPT and understands that actual AI doesn’t work like that, and if the task actually took 12 hours of crunching on tokens the bill would be an eye watering large number. So you can’t get away with faking your AI responses with a few humans doing the work.

There were also follow on stories where writers got confused about hybrid systems that had humans doing review and RLHF, thinking that any involvement of a human in the loop was equivalent of faking AI by having humans do the work. Most of the stories I saw toward the end of this trend were this style.

story_title.value: How the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” is deceiving

comment_text.value:
I believe we are at a crossroads here. The key question is: Do we want (desire or require) humans to understand the implementation?

If the answer is no, then AI agents producing code faster and "more correct" (in some arguably questionable sense but let's fly with the assumption for a moment) should be embraced fully. Take the humans out of the loop, why review code, if there is a problem later then just ask the next AI agent to fix it. Similar to not looking at generated code by a compiler. Iterate fast, don't look back. Some code bases and some entire companies have adopted this view.

If the answer is yes then we need to keep the human in the loop, ensure they have enough understanding to maintain the thing, review all the code etc. AI is just another tool to produce the code which ultimately the human still owns. Many code bases follow this philosophy.

It seems to me that the discussion always ultimately falls on one of these two sides. They are incompatible but you need to pick one. Depending on which you pick, it is easy to predict how you argue in such discussions.

story_title.value: Development statistics for the 7.2 kernel

comment_text.value:
The project is an attempt to automate the full market intelligence workflow, using fashion as first vertical, probably then to expand.

Process trigger is hourly industry news collection and selection, via Tavily and RSS feeds. Business selection rules dedupliaces and pick topics worth investigating. Then an agent with industry main KPIs list is in charge to figure out which metrics could help explain what's happening, given a constraint of viable sources (mainly web scraping), and determines what data to collect. Firecrawl handles scraping, other sources are internal. System structures data, run calculations, generate BI charts and insights, and publish the results.

The whole pipeline runs automatically, from identifying a market question to producing a data-backed analysis.

Additionally users may request custom reports, but this is non-essential to the service, which can be accessed without log in and without paid plans

The tricky part is - despite of the promise of most scraping tools like firecrawl and others, to affectively close the loop of data acquisition. not easy (we had to integrate it with data marketplaces with humans in the loop). We decided not to have an llm chat UI, not 100% sure of this choice, but - as of today - it is not present. Project is live at [https://tfb.databoutique.com](https://tfb.databoutique.com), with public analyses you can explore without signing up.

Feedback apreciated.

story_title.value: Show HN: We automated market Intel with a Statista-like engine for fashion

comment_text.value:
> In your code, this makes the model subtly devolve into certain patterns and stereotypes that aren't best practices, it's just a randomly frozen trajectory that is extremely hard to change zero-shot, without running a second pass.

But in practice, who uses models “zero-shot”? It is standard for coding agents to review their own code even before returning to the user — so a zero-shot agent invocation isn’t a zero-shot model invocation. And then many users will get a different run of the agent to review the change a(frequently even a different model being invoked by a different harness-e.g. I personally mix Claude, Copilot and Cursor)

> This is the reason everybody does the same thing.

If you have a human-in-the-loop reviewing the agent output, different humans will have different opinions on what the agent should have done instead, and they’ll tell the agent to redo its output in different ways. And then they tire of repeating themselves, and it becomes guidelines in AGENTS.md.

Additionally, a coding agent asked to add a feature to a large code base will frequently check for the code base’s existing design and coding patterns, and so will end up producing very different code than it would have given a blank slate.

story_title.value: Why do LLM pelicans look like this?

comment_text.value:
Before we had LLMs, we had product managers, project managers, scrum leaders, etc as roles on software engineering teams. I think as LLM-enabled development progresses we'll start to see these roles and the crossover to engineering continue to meld.

It's not like engineers didn't know that project management, voice of the customer, and organizing tasks as an intermediary between engineering and management was a thing that could/should/needed to be done. It was just a delegation of tasks before because there was more work than one person could do. Now, all of these roles can be partly offloaded to LLMs, but still having a human in the loop to guide engineering and interface to the business/customer will still be valuable.

Knowing what to build overall, what to build next, what's coming later, and how the product relates to the business goals is still very much a human endeavor.

story_title.value: Ask HN: What is the current trajectory of a senior engineer?
